thread.title: Value Tough To Pin Down - LiveXLive Media, Inc. (NASDAQ:LIVX)

author: SA Marketplace
title: Value Tough To Pin Down - LiveXLive Media, Inc. (NASDAQ:LIVX)
text:
2018 seems to be ending on the wrong note in the markets. December is setting the wrong kind of records, and Q4 has been a bumpy one in general. This is what happens in the stock market sometimes, but it's been easy to forget over the decade-long bull market.
We're using the end of the year as a chance to lift our heads, survey the market, and see what might be coming ahead. To do so, we're inviting our Marketplace authors to do a series of roundtables . 2018 was another steady growth year for the platform, and we have a lot of great voices on the Marketplace, so we wanted to share their perspective with you.
Our Year-End Marketplace Roundtable series will run through the first full market week in January. We'll feature ten different roundtable discussions, with expert panels chiming in on Tech, Energy, Dividends, Other Income strategies, Gold, Value Investing, Small-Caps, Alternative investing strategies, Biotech, and the Macro outlook.
This roundtable looks at value investing. Does the market volatility mean value is coming back into fashion? Has value investing changed? We asked our panel to sort through the investing approach and how it fits today's market. We have 18 panelists, which is too much to read in one sitting, so we are breaking this into two groups of nine, the first of which we published yesterday. Here's today's nine authors:
James Brumley , author of The Well Rounded Investor Olsny Freitas , author of Alpha Generating Society Mark Bern, CFA and Mycroft Friedrich , author of Friedrich Global Research Gregory Vousvounis , author of Cautiously Greedy Investor Labutes IR , author of The Financial Alpha Portfolio Quad 7 Capital , author of BAD BEAT Investing David J. Waldron , author of Main Street Value Investor Long Hill Road Capital , author of Bargain-Priced Compounders KCI Research Ltd. , author of The Contrarian Seeking Alpha: The second half of the year appeared to be renewed vindication for value investing in part, as high-fliers like the FAANG stocks pulled back. How do you view the current climate for value investing? James Brumley: It’s still ideal, and perhaps even more so right now in the shadow of the market’s implosion. Whether or not we slip into a bear market from here, the vulnerability of growth names (like FAANG stocks) has been made clear. Late-stage economic growth favors value names anyway, and the potential economic headwind even further prioritizes the safety and reliability value names generally offer.
Olsny Freitas: I don't think that the current climate is that much different. It's still hard to find catalyst driven value situations. On the other hand, the market seems to punish poor fundamentals a lot better. I think this provides a very nice climate for short ideas which I believe also fit in a value investing philosophy.
Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: The pendulum swings, but over the very long term value investing outperforms growth. So, we think the current climate is more of a return to normal than an anomaly. But, with technology becoming a dominate sector, growth will continue to be more popular for the foreseeable future compared to earlier periods. Our focus on growth at a reasonable value is the key to our consistency regardless of environment.
Gregory Vousvounis: The general market pull-back has created a lot of opportunities for capital deployment, especially in small and micro cap stocks. The market is once more become a fertile hunting ground for value investors.
Labutes IR: Even though I don’t invest in FAANG stocks as I’m specialized in the financial sector, I saw the hype around these stocks as typical behavior of a stock market bubble. This means that investors are now more focused on business fundamentals rather than hypothetical future growth, being an environment that should be better for value investing compared to growth.
Quad 7 Capital: There is a lot of truth to this. With a bull market that had raged on for a decade, value investing was a bit of an afterthought as investors chased growth opportunities, and rightfully did so. With the big names like Apple ( AAPL ), Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ) and the like suffering huge pullbacks in the H2 2018, value hunters have started to come out in more force. However, value investing opportunities are the cornerstone of what our company does and our service BAD BEAT Investing highlights. Both short-term value, and long-term stories. There is always an opportunity to find a beaten down name or sector that has been left for dead. With the recent volatility in the market, more and more opportunities are now appearing to start scaling into long-term positions in high quality names. Valuations are coming down, and there are names and sectors that are cheap. Overall, the climate has improved dramatically and the next two years should provide a real opportunity to scoop up quality companies at great prices.
David J. Waldron: As a bottom-up value investor, I often find quality companies trading at temporary bargain prices in all market cycles. No question that more of these opportunities present themselves during the occasional downturn or bear market cycle such as what we may be experiencing now.
Long Hill Road Capital: To me, value investing is about buying something for less than it is worth. That's true whether a business is growing quickly or not, is profitable or not, or is part of a widely used acronym or not. Certainly, the downturn in most stocks since October has created more opportunities. Part ownership of some of the world's best businesses are now available at bargain prices.
KCI Research: Value investing is historically out-of-favor, similar to the ten-year period from 1990-2000, and even though FAANG stocks pulled back in the second half of 2018, they still relatively outperformed, so we have not see a capital rotation yet, though this is coming.
SA: One theme of the current market is that it's hard to find traditional value, so investors looking for that are forced into value traps. Do you buy this, and why or why not? If you do buy it, how are you adjusting? James Brumley: Nope, I don’t buy it. I get the argument, but I’m not buying into the idea. The pros have a knack for labeling some value names ‘value traps’ when they’re really not, and just as often don’t identify value stocks that actually are value traps. Don’t sweat the name-calling. I’m not making an adjustment, per se. The only thing I’m doing is becoming pickier about the potential stories that can be told in support of a value-based pick. If the market doesn’t believe a value stock is worth owning, it’s not going to perform well – even if it should – in this pessimistic environment.
Olsny Freitas: Current market or not, I think value investing is as much about avoiding value traps as it is about investing in value. I think that a lot of yield chasers or overly quantitative folks make this mistake. The most common mistakes from a practical standpoint that I see value investors make:
Ignoring or oversimplifying debt and leverage. Not understanding the ebbs and flows of working capital and overstating operating cash flow as a result. A too quantitative approach without more holistic and qualitative considerations. Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: It is true that value investors can fall into value traps, but that is not unique to the current situation. Value traps occur all the time, but there are probably more likely to be found now and in the future due to the higher levels of disruption of traditional business models. There is also a lot of manipulation of earnings going on today that did not exist a decade ago. That is why we focus our analysis on free cash flow and GAAP reporting. We look for consistently superior reported results in free cash flow generation tied to consistent revenue growth. Our approach requires patience and rigorous analysis rather than trying to find ways to justify making questionable investments. We have proven that it is possible to outperform the major indices without being fully invested, holding as much as a third of a portfolio in cash to reduce risk.
Gregory Vousvounis: No I don't buy this. There are always opportunities out there. However, the investing game has become harder than just looking a screen and buying stocks that trade below book value. Nevertheless there are stocks that are cheaper than they look and offer a good margin of safety. You just have to find them. And a note on value traps. There is no such thing. A stock is cheap either because it should be or because it is mispriced. Both Microsoft ( MSFT ) and Sears ( OTCPK:SHLDQ ) were once labeled as "value traps". One became the most valuable stock in the market and the other went bankrupt. You are either right or wrong on an investment and some times it takes several years to know which one it is.
Labutes IR: I agree to that, despite the recent market sell-off, it is hard to find good companies at bargain prices. This means that most shares that trade at low valuations have structural problems, rather than being mispriced. A classical example within my coverage is Deutsche Bank ( DB ), trading at a depressed valuation and being in my opinion a value trap.
Quad 7 Capital: We do not subscribe to this notion, despite there being some truth to the assertion. No investor should feel compelled to buy stocks simply because they look cheap. Sometimes investors feel a need to push the envelope and start scooping shares in a stock that is falling because there is a fear of missing out, or FOMO, on a bounce. Let us be very clear here. If the market falls another 25-30% next year, then EVERY stock is a value trap. This is because they will all fall. More generally, we believe the onus is on opinion makers, here at Seeking Alpha and elsewhere, to be diligent in their recommendations for value. We have seen frequently that stocks are being recommended as value that fail to meet our rigorous standards for traditional value from a longer-term perspective. Metrics such as earnings multiples, forward PEG ratios, price-to-sales, EBITDA growth, dividend growth and yield, payout ratios, leverage, and sector pressures and competition to name just a few. We have seen a number of value calls made that see opportunity in some of these metrics while others are red flags. Some food companies and retail names come to mind. Low quality businesses lack the competitive advantages that allow for high returns on capital, yet we often see these pushed as 'value'. These are the traps. These companies have average or poor financial returns because intense competition drives down returns for everyone in that sector. Growth prospects are limited, so any cash the company does generate often gets burnt at worst. At best you get some dividends or share repurchases. These businesses tend to make poor long-term investments and can easily end up causing permanent losses. Make sure you are looking at the whole picture. Cheap can always get cheaper. We ourselves fell into this a bit in the semiconductor space with Micron ( MU ) and Applied Materials ( AMAT ) earlier this year. Great value at the time, even better now, but we were overzealous. Don't feel compelled to buy and hold because it "looks cheap."
David J. Waldron: Value traps and falling knives are unavoidable consequences of stock-picking. The challenge is to consistently apply thought, discipline, patience, and a pinch of common sense to ultimately find more enduring good ideas than good ideas "at the time." Assuming equal allocation, if 3 or 4 out five ideas are profitable, the losses from the 1 or 2 not so good ideas are more likely to be offset or covered by the winners.
Long Hill Road Capital: I'm not sure about that. I've seen more traditional value investors expand their universe to include businesses that optically look more expensive. These tend to be faster growing businesses that trade at higher multiples, but where one can make a case that they are undervalued. Often this is because growth investments through the income statement depress current earnings, making them look more expensive than they really are.
KCI Research: If you look closely at what many investors are identifying as value stocks, it is clear they are settling. This is what the market does. It forces extremes, and thus very few are ultimately positioned for the best opportunities.
SA: On the flipside, many value investors have given up on traditional value investing and tilted towards 'quality' or 'compounders.' Again, what do you think about this direction, and how have you adjusted, adopted, or avoided this? James Brumley: That’s not exactly a new direction. It’s just newly been given labels. That’s fine. But, as before, it’s far more fruitful to buy a name just because it’s a good company that the market can believe in than it is to try and fill an arbitrary void in a portfolio. It just so happens that the best value names are largely going to be the ‘compounders’ you mentioned.
Olsny Freitas: I think that I have a slightly different philosophy on what value investing is. To me, it is simply a high-conviction, catalyst-driven situation that provides an asymmetric risk-reward profile. The margin of safety here is implied. I don't care for things like 'quality' or 'compounders'. I simply require value so I don't think I could tell you or anyone the difference between 'traditional', 'quality' or 'compounder' value investing.
Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: Our approach to investing has always focused on quality companies but we only invest when we find exceptional value in terms of future growth potential relative to the current valuation. We are very picky and require consistently superior execution and results at a price that increases the probability of long-term successful investing results. But quality is always the most important aspect of any company that we are willing to include in one of our four portfolios (focused growth, conservative growth, dividend growth, and aggressive growth). We never consider a poorly run company at any price.
Gregory Vousvounis: Changing one's style is something not to be done lightly. Usually, the best time to adopt a strategy is after it has fallen out of favor. If you cannot find opportunities that fit your style then one the following is usually true:
You are not looking at the right place and/or you are not looking hard enough. We are at a market extreme (top or bottom) and you should prepare for mean reversion. That said, changing strategies successfully is what distinguishes great investors from the simply good ones. Everyone should be trying to expand their circle of competence but should do it slowly and very conservatively because it is very easy to step out of it and get smoked.
Labutes IR: I have adapted my investment methodology to integrate multiple factors in my investment process, combining value with growth at a reasonable price, quality and income. This has allowed me to have better returns across the market cycle than compared to just following a traditional value investing approach.
Quad 7 Capital: Value investing isn't one size fits all. As we have alluded to, we have both a short-term and long-term outlook to value. In a ten-year bull market, select sectors have been punished and offered value, but these were largely ignored by many who went after quality and growth. In terms of buying compounders/quality, there is nothing wrong with this. In fact, we encourage it, to a degree. While investing in diverse sectors and holdings is wise, one of the things we tell our members is that having a diverse strategy to investing is perhaps more important.
If your goal is to maximize your wealth over the next decade or two, investing in high quality compounders is your best bet. Compounders have many advantages. They have often have competitive advantages that allow for sustainably high returns on your investment. We actually think this approach is underappreciated by value investors generally. Oddly, this can allow these stocks to trade very cheaply at times, but will be ignored because the traditional metrics make them look 'expensive.' If there is one thing we could urge value investors to think about, it is that earnings multiples are all relative to the sector, the company, and the market. This is largely ignored. Many value investors see a 20 times earnings multiple and think the stock is expensive. Wrong. It cannot be deemed expensive if you do not investigate its valuation which often can be more than justified by the company's future reinvestment opportunities and sector strength.
In fact, at BAD BEAT Investing, we would ballpark that 50% of the opportunities we find are these types of names. Hidden value in plain sight! Despite looking expensive on the surface, these stocks can offer immense long-term value. We can see why many would abandon traditional value investing in favor of this approach, but again, it is about balance. With the current market, we think there is room for both traditional value hunting, and more hidden value discovery.
David J. Waldron: Perhaps there are diverging interpretations of "traditional value investing" which I deem as quality compounders purchased at reasonable prices. "Value trading" would be more in line with buying "cigar buts" or stocks of lower quality companies on speculation, then selling based on an anticipated, i.e., hoped for, corporate, industry, or macro event.
Long Hill Road Capital: So many successful investors have evolved from cigar-butt investing to high-quality compounder investing. Buffett is the obvious example, and I think it's an intelligent evolution if truly long-term investing fits your temperament. If you want to hold a stock for 10+ years, your returns will be more influenced by management's capital allocation decisions and returns on incremental invested capital ("ROIIC") than by how cheaply you may have bought the shares. On the other hand, if you hold a cigar butt for 10+ years, you're probably not going to make a good annualized return even if you bought it at a big discount. I want to own businesses for 10+ years, so I'd much rather own a business that is often founder-led, that has a small market share of a very big addressable market, and that has the competitive advantages required to capitalize on that growth opportunity. In a perfect world, I'll buy the stock after some temporary problem that has caused the stock to crater. At that point, it's out-of-favor, left for dead, and the expectations baked into the stock price are very achievable, if not easily beatable. Think TripAdvisor (NASDAQ: TRIP ) (NASDAQ: LTRPA ) (NASDAQ: LTRPB ) at $30 per share in 2017. You may have guessed all that since my Marketplace service is called Bargain-Priced Compounders.
KCI Research: Historically, the best performing stocks in the stock market universe are small-cap value stocks. There are plenty of opportunities in this area of the market today, but the sectors these opportunities are in are unpalatable to most investors, so for this reason, the opportunities are even bigger, similar in scope to how REITs were out-of-favor in the late 1990s, but then outperformed for far longer than anyone would have thought.
SA: What do you enjoy about this approach to investing? James Brumley: I get to sleep (a little) at night.
Olsny Freitas: That there's a very explorer or detective type feel to the process.
Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: In one word: consistency. Our portfolio companies consistently generate free cash flow return on invested capital at rates far greater than the average of S&P component companies. We remain confident that our companies will outperform over the long term, even when one or two may hit a rough patch, because of the quality of earnings and pristine balance sheets along with superior management. Market corrections just give us the opportunity to add shares of the best companies at better valuations.
Gregory Vousvounis: It allows me to sleep at night and keep my convictions, no matter what the market does.
Treating stocks properly (as what they are, pieces of a business) allows for a more confident approach. When using this method the market becomes a servant instead of a master and disagreeing with it is normal and desirable not agonizing and foolhardy.
Labutes IR: I like to find good businesses with mispriced share prices, this allows me to have a long-term approach to investing and not be worried about short-term market volatility, as over the long-term the business fundamentals should prevail against short-term thinking and market sentiment
Quad 7 Capital: We love the fact that we can offer short-term, market beating returns through short-term plays in names that have been crushed. We enjoy the fact that we can find beaten down sectors and stocks that are offering traditional real value, cheap multiples, decent earnings growth, and perhaps a dividend. We like finding compounders that are offering hidden value, and while these are harder to come by, they make for great moves. Overall, we think a diversified portfolio and a diversified approach is the best winning strategy in the long run.
David J. Waldron: Long view value investing contributes to socioeconomic opportunities for my family, country, and the world by taking ownership slices of wonderful companies over an extended period, if not forever. Arguably buy-and-hold value investing is out of favor on Wall Street – as well as on Seeking Alpha in my observations – but it gives the thoughtful, disciplined, and patient, self-directed investor an exceptional opportunity to fund the significant milestones in life such as buying a home, paying for a college education, pursuing a passion, starting a business, or enjoying a comfortable retirement. Nevertheless, like Rome, life-changing portfolios are not built in a day.
Long Hill Road Capital: Long-term investing fits my personality. I have higher odds of success if I identify a great business, pay the right price, and then do nothing. I enjoy watching Amazon plant seeds in India years ago, or TripAdvisor reinvest in its Experiences business when it was nascent, or Alphabet ( GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) reinvest in Waymo today. It is rewarding to me to see these investments grow into big businesses, knowing I invested years prior at much lower prices. Plus, I think this sort of investing is less competitive because so few people have the temperament or type of capital to make these long-term investments. In contrast, the idea of "turning over as many rocks" as possible looking for any cheap asset just doesn't interest me. I'd rather go a mile deep understanding one great business than an inch deep understanding 50 average businesses.
KCI Research: Nothing right now. Ask me after the turn. On a serious note, you have to be able to endure pain and suffering to be a good value investor, and this axiom has certainly been true for much of the current bull market.
SA: Why will you practice value investing in 2019, and how? James Brumley: Well, to be clear, I’m not 100% exposed to value right now in any of my portfolios, and probably won’t be fully exposed in 2019. I’ve got more than a little growth exposure too, though I’m lamenting most of it. It’s just the nature of the beast.
To answer the question though, I’m very value-minded as we get 2019 going largely because value names have underperformed growth in a huge way since the end of 2014. Before the recent implosion, growth was up as much as 58% for the four-year span, and value was only up 25%. Both have been beaten down since then, but I think when the rebound arrives, value will take the lead.
Olsny Freitas: To me, value investing is simply the search for value. Maybe that is an arbitrage situation, or an undervalued distressed asset whether that is debt or equity. Maybe that is a short idea. However, above all, I require a catalyst and a high probability of analyzing the consequences of that catalyst correctly.
Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: We will stay the course by investing only in the companies that consistently produce excellent results and generate well above average free cash flow when priced at what we determine to be bargain prices. Due to the increased volatility we are experiencing, we will be patient and add only the best stocks with the greatest potential for future growth when the volatility begins to subside. Patience is the key to successful long-term value investing.
Gregory Vousvounis: Because it is the investing approach that better suits my character.
Labutes IR: Given the recent global economic slowdown and increased market volatility, value should perform better than growth or momentum in 2019, being therefore a good approach to protect capital in the next year. I will look for stocks that have been recently punished by the stock market, but have strong fundamentals and should do well if we don’t have a bear market in the next few months.
Quad 7 Capital: Given the way the end of 2018 is shaping up, we are likely to enter 2019 under more pressure. This will set up an abundance of what we like to call 'bad-beats', while putting enough pressure on quality companies to drive their stocks down to value, and hopefully deep value levels. Hidden value levels will also pop up. So we will employ a diversified approach to value across the various methods we have discussed above. One of the other key components to our strategy will be position sizing. While we generally do not recommend directly sizing considerations, we will likely target levels of purchasing stocks in companies we are interested in through pyramid style blocks (i.e., buy progressively more shares at predefined levels in a stock) so long as the story fundamentally remains the same. This approach will help take into account the risk for a declining overall market.
David J. Waldron: I will practice in 2019 what I have practiced for the past ten years in outperforming Mr. Market: screening for and researching quality, dividend-paying companies trading at reasonable prices and then holding a fractional slice of that enterprise for as long as it remains a quality operator. I have learned through trial and error that equating stock ownership to partnering with the company's board and employees in providing customers with in-demand products or services based on strong fundamentals and current value remains an enduring, profitable, and satisfying way to invest. The alternatives involve trading in and out of faceless stocks based on technical charts, market sentiment, trend following, momentum growth, high yield dividends, precision price targets, growth projections, quarterly performance, or any other of the myriad of noise preached daily on Wall Street with often dubious outcomes. That is because the Wall Street fee machine profits little on buy-and-hold investing, but continues to rake fees and commissions on the ever-popular, short-sighted trading platforms.
KCI Research: Why? There are generational return opportunities. How? With a clear mind, looking forward, and forgetting about the past two years.
SA: What was the big story or lesson learned for you in 2018? James Brumley: The same lesson that every investor has to learn over and over again… never turn your back on the market, and don’t trust headlines. The pros were resoundingly, collectively bullish through October. Apparently, much has changed in the meantime. Every other year or so the market throws an unexpected curve ball we all should have actually been expecting.
Olsny Freitas: To me, the big lesson of 2018 is that you have to be able to adapt. While the writing was perhaps a bit on the wall, the last couple of months of 2018 were brutal for many investors. Unless you managed to switch and recognize that perhaps a higher short exposure is the wise thing to do.
More importantly, I'm very proud of my method as it seems to have guided me through very successfully. Once the long value opportunities dried up, I simply started picking high conviction shorts. These short ideas have averaged 30% this year. If I had forced myself to see value just because I 'am' a value investor, I would've probably been adding to lows.
Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: Our research team has over 75 years of experience, and between the two of us, we have seen it all several times over. This year has been a year of great volatility probably because 2017 was not. Normally there is a correction in stocks, on average, once a year with the average drawdown being about 14.5%. In 2017, there were no dips in the major indices of much over 4%, if that, so it was the “abnormal” year. This year investors merely paid for the easy ride that was 2017. The market moves sideways for one of two reasons: either to consolidate and build a base from which to move higher or as a preamble to the next major recessionary period. It is not yet clear which result we will see but something very interesting is coming in 2019. By holding only high quality stocks and a lot of cash in our model portfolios, we believe we are well positioned for whatever happens.
Gregory Vousvounis: In 2018, I was reminded how irrational the market can get. From absurdly high valuations for mega caps in Q1 to Q3 to absurdly cheap valuations for small-cap and micro-cap stocks in Q4. We should never forget that the market is here to serve us, not guide us.
Labutes IR: That being a contrarian requires a lot of patience and self-discipline. I was somewhat bearish for the stock market, and the financial sector, since the first quarter of this year and this took some time to pay off. This was a strong reason why I have launched the Financials Alpha Portfolio marketplace service using a Long/Short strategy, something that was proven right over the past three months.
Quad 7 Capital: While we only touch on some of the technical side of our approaches in our public articles, we think we will be more diligent in protecting capital through defensive strategies and taking on more short-oriented positions where appropriate. While that may sound strange coming from a value-oriented firm, this can simply mean having some protective puts against core positions. When we saw terrible news in technology in the charts, we wish we were more diligent in getting out in front of it by playing some defense. While we started raising cash in early September 2018, we wish we were a bit more proactive in this sector as many of our losing plays were focused here, and that cost us, and our members some money.
David J. Waldron: 2018 was another reminder that value prevails in all market cycles. Both my large-cap and small-cap total return portfolios are cumulatively outperforming their respective benchmarks (S&P 500 and Russell 2000) including on the downside. Maintaining a wide margin of safety remains a crucial factor of successful value investing. Protect your principal upfront against the unpredictable yet unavoidable downturns, and the upside will usually take care of itself.
Long Hill Road Capital: As cheap as I thought some of my holdings were, they can get a lot cheaper.
KCI Research: Embedded trends in the market are extraordinarily strong, as almost all investors have become either momentum investors, traders, or dividend growth investors.
SA: What is one of your best ideas for 2019, and what is the story? James Brumley: It’s not a value stock, ironically enough, but right now I like Intercept Pharmaceuticals ( ICPT ) here. The company isn’t yet profitable, but revenue is growing rapidly and the losses are shrinking fast as its liver disease drug Ocaliva gains traction. It’s still in the very early innings for the therapy, but the potential is significant just because there’s so little head-to-head competition. It’s neither growth nor value, which should keep it out of the value-vs.-growth duel and let it do its own non-cyclical thing.
Olsny Freitas: I've got a couple that I like. I'd say iPic Entertainment ( IPIC ) or LiveXLive Media ( LIVX ) are high conviction shorts. These companies will most likely not exist within 16 months or will do so in severely diminished value (-50% -80%). On the long side, I have Transglobe Energy Corp. ( TGA ), the stock was up over 160% since I recommended it and has now drifted down to slightly above its starting position. Since I had taken some profits in the 100% range, I think this is a great idea to recycle as the fundamentals have only improved and significantly so. I expect TGA to deliver a 100% return in 2019 as well.
Mark Bern and Mycroft Friedrich: We think that Apple offers great upside potential from the current price. Tremendous free cash flow generation, a few more years of the current upgrade cycle in iPhones and strong, double digit revenue growth from its services (with high margins) are just some of the reasons we like the stock for 2019.
Apple has more flexibility than probably any other company due to its incredible free cash flow generation. The company is committed to returning profits to its shareholders by increasing its dividend and buying back shares.
The company also has the wherewithal to spend heavily on R&D. Naysayers quibble about no new big products coming out but are missing the point. Products, like the iPhone, are not necessary to continue growth in revenues and cash generation. The next phase of growth will be led by Apple's services as it reaches critical mass. The iPhone isn't dead but, rather, it will be the cash cow that funds growth in other areas.
Gregory Vousvounis: My best idea is somewhat unconventional. It is a new company with a little more than a year of life. RumbleON ( RMBL ) is an online marketplace where consumers can sell their used motorcycle or car either by accepting the company's cash offer or by listing it to be bought be other consumers.
The vehicles that are bought by RumbleON are sold either to dealers or to other consumers through the internet. RumbleON is one of its kind as it is the only national online marketplace for used vehicles. The company is currently expanding to cars and they plan to sell every type of vehicle that has a VIN.
The company is building a moat based on scale as it is aggregating the used vehicles supply and is doing it by gaining consumer trust and offering good prices. It has found product-market fit as its revenues have exploded within its first year of operation and through its recent acquisition has become cash flow positive. I thing that RumbleON is a low risk play with multi-bagger potential.
Labutes IR: One of my best ideas right now for 2019 is Danske Bank ( OTCPK:DNSKF ) ( OTCPK:DNSKY ), a quality bank in the Nordics countries that has been heavily punished by investors due to a unit of its business being used for money laundering a few years ago. This has spooked investors about potential litigation costs, leading to mispricing considering the bank’s strong fundamentals. If the bank (as I expect) is able to settle this for a manageable amount, its shares have a lot of upside as litigation risk would disappear and investors could value the bank again based on its earnings power.
Quad 7 Capital: Coming into 2019 we are a bit torn, and may actually be going back to replaying a past idea. That said, we have a few ideas to consider for value.
The first idea is playing Southwestern Energy ( SWN ). Look, oil prices fell, but natural gas prices have moved higher at out month contract pricing remains solid. While it is the long-term view on natural gas that is the reason a lot of these names trade at discount, we see so much value in this name at $3.50 a share again (the price at the time of this response). In just over a month and a half, nearly 45% of the stock's value has been wiped out. The basic story here is that natural gas prices, while likely to fall back to $3 or so, have been up. The oil price decline is temporary, it will come back, as always. Only a fraction of SWN's revenues are oil related, some are liquids, and the rest is nat gas. The company was thriving at sub-$3 gas, and will continue to do so. It has sold off assets, is repurchasing shares, and is delevering to improve its balance sheet and is shifting its focus a bit. It's trading at less than 4X 2019 EPS projections now. Talk about value.
The second name we think its time for every value investor to consider is AT&T ( T ). The debt is being tackled. The dividend continues to be raised as cash flows are growing. The purchase of Time Warner has made this a bit of a global entertainment and communications play. We think at $29 here, the stock is offering compelling value. While EPS growth is probably the biggest concern following the debt, cash flows continue to expand. It's a value play with a dividend growth and income aspect. We think shares will see support as investors shift to defense.
Finally, we think Philip Morris ( PM ) is offering a compelling entry point at 6.6% yield based on its current price of under $69 a share. While we know traditional cigarette sales are declining, heated tobacco products are making up for volumes and driving revenues and EPS higher. We expect the stock to rebound in 2019 as value investors and dividend growth investors seek this bargain price. Of course, should the market roll over further, all stocks will come down, but we think this name is a great defensive play and one that should be held for the long-term.
Long Hill Road Capital: Amazon is one of the world's best businesses, it is run by the best CEO in the world, according to Warren Buffett, and its stock is very cheap right now at $1,474 per share. The growth of global e-commerce and the growth of the public cloud market are inevitable long-term trends, and Amazon is leading the way in both. Amazon is just getting started in its high-margin ad business, and will likely create big new businesses from scratch in global logistics, health care, and several other ventures we don't know much about yet. The culture is relentlessly focused on pleasing the customer, and you can see the benefits of that in its incredible customer loyalty. That gives Amazon "permission" from the customer to enter almost any category. I like to do a lot of scenario analysis with very explicit long-term assumptions. My Bear, Base, and Bull case per-share valuations for AMZN are $1,597, $2,113, and $2,985. So at $1,474 per share today, the market is discounting a scenario that is more pessimistic than my Bear case. I think the market underestimates Amazon's long-term margin profile because it underestimates how much reinvestment spending is occurring and depressing margins. I'll also point out none of my scenarios include any value for any big new business Amazon may build in the future. If you look at the company's history and culture, that is a very conservative assumption.
KCI Research: My ninth best idea right now on a potential appreciation potential basis, with a more than 200% potential return to my calculated intrinsic fair value is U.S. Steel ( X ). Earning estimates more than doubled for U.S. Steel for 2018, and 2019, from the start of 2018, yet the stock is down almost 50% as of the writing. Normally, increases in earnings estimates are highly correlated with an increasing stock price. Not this year. For U.S. Steel, they are very cheap on traditional valuation rations, with a forward price-to-earnings ratio below 5, and debt has come down materially since 2015, so much so that their balance sheet is actually pretty strong. Ideas that rank above U.S. Steel in my proprietary rankings generally have to do with the energy sector.
